label: M9 S8 | The Valuation Multiple Formula Arsenal

formulas.name: P/E Ratio
formulas.formula: P/E = Market Price per Share / Earnings per Share = Market Cap / Net Profit

variables.meaning: Current trading price of one share
Earnings Per Share = Net Profit / Number of Outstanding Shares

formulas.worked_example: Nestle India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,20,000 Cr. Net Profit ≈ ₹2,390 Cr. P/E = 2,20,000 / 2,390 = 92x (approximately). Nestle is one of the most expensive stocks in India on P/E basis. Compare Coal India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,30,000 Cr. Net Profit ≈ ₹36,500 Cr. P/E = 2,30,000 / 36,500 = 6.3x. Coal India is one of the cheapest large-caps in India on P/E basis. Same absolute market cap, radically different multiples — because the market prices growth (Nestle's 10-12% CAGR), stability (consumer staples survive recessions), and moat (brand premium) very differently from cyclicality (coal prices), policy risk (government regulation), and structural disruption (renewables replacing coal).
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/E is the most intuitive multiple but also the most dangerous. It breaks for loss-making companies (division by near-zero), for banks (provisioning distorts earnings year-to-year), for companies with heavy one-off items, and for comparisons across companies with different capital structures. Use with care and always cross-check with EV-based multiples.

formulas.name: P/B Ratio
formulas.formula: P/B = Market Price / Book Value per Share = Market Cap / Shareholders' Equity

variables.meaning: Current market value of all outstanding equity
Book Value = Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus

formulas.worked_example: HDFC Bank FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹8,70,000 Cr. Shareholders' Equity ≈ ₹2,80,000 Cr. P/B = 8,70,000 / 2,80,000 = 3.1x. HDFC Bank is the gold standard of Indian private banking, trading at over 3 times book — a premium to the sector median of ~2x and well above PSU banks (many of which trade at below 1x). State Bank of India FY23: P/B ≈ 1.3x. IndusInd Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 1.6x. Kotak Mahindra Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 3.5x. PSU banks (Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank): P/B 0.7-1.0x. The P/B differential across Indian banks exactly reflects the market's view of return quality (ROE), asset quality (NPAs), and growth potential.
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/B is the right lens for banks because banks' 'earnings' fluctuate with provisioning cycles, but their book value — the actual net assets — is a stable anchor. For non-financial businesses, P/B is less useful because book value doesn't capture brand, technology, or goodwill. An Infosys or TCS trading at 15x P/B doesn't mean they're expensive — their book value simply doesn't reflect the economic value of their human capital and client relationships.

formulas.name: Enterprise Value (EV)
formulas.formula: EV = Market Cap + Total Debt + Preferred Equity + Minority Interest - Cash and Cash Equivalents

variables.meaning: Current market value of common equity
Short-term debt + Long-term debt + Current portion of long-term debt
Cash + Cash equivalents + Liquid investments

formulas.worked_example: Reliance Industries FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹17,00,000 Cr. Total Debt ≈ ₹3,10,000 Cr. Cash ≈ ₹85,000 Cr. Minority Interest ≈ ₹1,30,000 Cr. EV = 17,00,000 + 3,10,000 + 1,30,000 - 85,000 = ₹20,55,000 Cr. So while the market cap is ₹17 lakh crore, the full enterprise value — what it would cost to acquire all of Reliance's capital claims — is ₹20.55 lakh crore. This is especially important for valuation comparisons because a company with less debt would have a lower EV relative to its market cap, making direct EV/EBITDA comparisons meaningful.
formulas.sensitivity_note: EV is the 'true cost of acquiring the business' because if you bought the company, you would inherit its debt (added to cost) and could use its cash (subtracted from cost). This makes EV far more accurate than Market Cap for cross-company comparisons. Forgetting to subtract cash or add debt is the most common valuation error beginners make.

formulas.name: EV/EBITDA

variables.meaning: Enterprise Value as defined above
Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation

formulas.worked_example: Asian Paints FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,90,000 Cr. EBITDA ≈ ₹6,800 Cr. EV/EBITDA = 42.6x. Extraordinarily rich — reflects the market's confidence in Asian Paints' 30%+ ROCE moat and durable growth. Compare Tata Steel FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,50,000 Cr. EBITDA ≈ ₹28,000 Cr. EV/EBITDA = 8.9x. Classic cyclical valuation — the market refuses to pay a premium for commodity earnings because steel prices can collapse at any cycle turn. Rule of thumb benchmarks: cyclical commodity businesses 5-10x, stable manufacturing 10-14x, consumer staples 25-45x, luxury consumer and premium brands 40-60x, software/tech 25-50x depending on growth.
formulas.sensitivity_note: EV/EBITDA is the professional's default because it is capital-structure neutral and ignores non-cash depreciation. It works well for cross-company comparison. However, it understates the true cost of capex-heavy businesses (where depreciation is real economic cost). For capex-heavy industries, also look at EV/EBIT.

formulas.name: PEG Ratio
formulas.formula: PEG = P/E Ratio / Expected Earnings Growth Rate (%)

variables.meaning: Current or forward P/E ratio
Expected annual EPS growth rate, usually 2-3 year CAGR

formulas.worked_example: A growth company with P/E of 30 and expected earnings growth of 25% per year: PEG = 30/25 = 1.2. Mildly expensive but close to fair for a growth stock. Peter Lynch's rule: PEG below 1 is potentially cheap, PEG above 2 is expensive. Compare Coal India: P/E of 6, expected growth of 5%: PEG = 6/5 = 1.2. Technically the same PEG as the growth company — illustrating why PEG must be interpreted alongside business quality. A growth business at PEG 1.2 is attractive; a cyclical commodity business at PEG 1.2 is not, because the growth is unreliable.
formulas.sensitivity_note: PEG works beautifully for growth stocks with predictable earnings trajectories but breaks down for cyclicals, turnarounds, or businesses with unreliable forward estimates. Always use multi-year (3-year+) growth estimates rather than single-year growth to avoid being fooled by one-off spikes.

formulas.name: P/S Ratio (Price-to-Sales)

variables.meaning: Current equity value
Trailing 12-month or forward annual revenue

formulas.worked_example: Zomato FY23 (at listing): Market Cap at IPO ≈ ₹64,000 Cr. Revenue ≈ ₹4,200 Cr. P/S = 64,000 / 4,200 = 15x. Compare Amazon historical P/S during early growth years: 4-6x. Zomato at 15x P/S meant the market was assigning significant growth optionality to future food delivery expansion — partially realised, partially not. P/S is the go-to multiple for loss-making growth companies where P/E is meaningless.
formulas.sensitivity_note: P/S ignores margin differences — a company with 30% operating margin and one with 5% margin can trade at similar P/S but have vastly different intrinsic values. Use P/S only as a starting point for loss-making companies; always overlay margin expectations before concluding.

formulas.name: P/E Ratio
formulas.formula: P/E = Market Price per Share / Earnings per Share = Market Cap / Net Profit

variables.meaning: Current trading price of one share
Earnings Per Share = Net Profit / Number of Outstanding Shares

formulas.plain_english: The P/E ratio tells you how many rupees of market value investors are willing to pay for every rupee of annual earnings. A high P/E suggests the market expects strong future growth or prizes stability and competitive moat; a low P/E suggests either cyclical weakness, investor pessimism, or genuine value. It is intuitive but can be misleading for loss-making companies, banks with volatile provisions, or firms with large one-off items.

worked_example.problem: Compare the valuation of two large-cap Indian companies with identical market capitalisation but vastly different earnings profiles.
steps: Nestle India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,20,000 Cr, Net Profit ≈ ₹2,390 Cr → P/E = 2,20,000 / 2,390 ≈ 92x
Coal India FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹2,30,000 Cr, Net Profit ≈ ₹36,500 Cr → P/E = 2,30,000 / 36,500 ≈ 6.3x

Interpret the differential: Nestle commands a premium multiple because of its 10–12% CAGR growth expectation, pricing power (consumer staples moat), and defensive characteristics (recession-resistant). Coal India trades at a depressed multiple due to cyclicality (coal prices fluctuate), policy risk, and structural headwinds from the energy transition to renewables.
worked_example.result: Same absolute market cap (₹2.2–2.3 lakh crore), but P/E multiples differ 14-fold, illustrating how the market prices growth, stability, and competitive moat versus cyclicality and disruption risk.
worked_example.insight: P/E is intuitive but context-dependent. Always compare multiples within the same industry or against companies with similar growth and risk profiles. A 92x P/E for Nestle is reasonable for a 30-year moat; a 92x P/E for a cyclical company would signal dangerous overvaluation.

formulas.sensitivity_note: P/E is the most intuitive multiple but also the most dangerous. It breaks for loss-making companies (division by near-zero), for banks (provisioning distorts earnings year-to-year), for companies with heavy one-off items, and for comparisons across companies with different capital structures. Use with care and always cross-check with EV-based multiples.

formulas.name: P/B Ratio
formulas.formula: P/B = Market Price / Book Value per Share = Market Cap / Shareholders' Equity

variables.meaning: Current market value of all outstanding equity
Book Value = Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus

formulas.plain_english: The P/B ratio compares what investors are willing to pay for equity to the accounting book value of that equity. For banks, P/B is particularly valuable because it reflects the market's view of the bank's return on equity (ROE) and asset quality independent of provisioning noise. For tech or service companies, P/B is less reliable because book value ignores intangible value like brand, patents, and human capital.

worked_example.problem: Compare valuation premiums and asset quality across Indian banks using P/B ratios.
steps: HDFC Bank FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹8,70,000 Cr, Shareholders' Equity ≈ ₹2,80,000 Cr → P/B = 8,70,000 / 2,80,000 = 3.1x
State Bank of India FY23: P/B ≈ 1.3x
IndusInd Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 1.6x
Kotak Mahindra Bank FY23: P/B ≈ 3.5x
PSU banks (Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank): P/B ≈ 0.7–1.0x

Interpret: HDFC and Kotak trade at 3–3.5x book (premium), reflecting high ROE, strong asset quality, and growth optionality. SBI trades at 1.3x (sector median ~2x), reflecting lower ROE and regulatory constraints. PSU banks trade below 1x, indicating market pessimism about NPAs, ROE recovery, or government ownership overhang.
worked_example.result: P/B multiples for Indian banks range from 0.7x (PSU banks) to 3.5x (Kotak), directly mirroring the market's assessment of profitability quality, credit risk, and growth prospects.
worked_example.insight: For banks, P/B is the anchor metric because book value (equity capital) is stable, but earnings are distorted by provisioning cycles. A private bank at 3x book with 15%+ ROE is more fairly valued than a PSU bank at 0.8x book with 8% ROE, because the multiple reflects genuine franchise quality.

formulas.sensitivity_note: P/B is the right lens for banks because banks' 'earnings' fluctuate with provisioning cycles, but their book value — the actual net assets — is a stable anchor. For non-financial businesses, P/B is less useful because book value doesn't capture brand, technology, or goodwill. An Infosys or TCS trading at 15x P/B doesn't mean they're expensive — their book value simply doesn't reflect the economic value of their human capital and client relationships.

formulas.name: Enterprise Value (EV)
formulas.formula: EV = Market Cap + Total Debt + Preferred Equity + Minority Interest - Cash and Cash Equivalents

variables.meaning: Current market value of common equity
Short-term debt + Long-term debt + Current portion of long-term debt
Cash + Cash equivalents + Liquid investments
Market value of preferred shares (if any)
Market value of non-controlling interests in consolidated subsidiaries

formulas.plain_english: Enterprise Value is the total economic value of a business, representing the cost to acquire all claims on its assets (debt, preferred stock, common equity) net of cash that could repay debt. Unlike market cap, EV is capital-structure neutral, making it the right foundation for comparing businesses with different leverage. This is why EV-based multiples (EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue) are far more reliable for peer comparison than equity multiples.
computation: 1. Identify and sum: Market Cap + Total Debt + Preferred Equity + Minority Interest
2. Subtract: Cash and Cash Equivalents (this nets out the debt that cash could immediately repay)
3. The result is the net enterprise value — the true cost of acquiring all operating assets

worked_example.problem: Calculate the full enterprise value of a large Indian industrial conglomerate and understand why it differs materially from market cap.
steps: Reliance Industries FY23: Market Cap ≈ ₹17,00,000 Cr
Add Total Debt: ₹3,10,000 Cr (borrowings to finance capex and operations)
Add Minority Interest: ₹1,30,000 Cr (consolidated subsidiary interests Reliance doesn't own 100% of)
Subtract Cash: ₹85,000 Cr (net available to repay debt)
worked_example.result: Reliance's market cap is ₹17 lakh crore, but its enterprise value is ₹20.55 lakh crore — a difference of ₹3.55 lakh crore, representing the net leverage (debt minus cash) and minority claims.
worked_example.insight: A buyer acquiring Reliance would pay the market cap to equity holders, but would also inherit ₹3.25 lakh crore net debt (gross debt minus cash). EV is thus the true economic cost of control, and using it for multiples ensures comparisons across companies with different capital structures are apples-to-apples.

formulas.sensitivity_note: EV is the 'true cost of acquiring the business' because if you bought the company, you would inherit its debt (added to cost) and could use its cash (subtracted from cost). This makes EV far more accurate than Market Cap for cross-company comparisons. Forgetting to subtract cash or add debt is the most common valuation error beginners make.

formulas.name: EV/EBITDA

variables.meaning: Enterprise Value as calculated above
Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation; represents operating cash-generation power before financing and non-cash charges

formulas.plain_english: EV/EBITDA is the professional's go-to multiple because it isolates the value of operating assets without distortion from capital structure, taxes, or accounting depreciation assumptions. It answers: 'How many years of operating cash flow (EBITDA) is the market paying for this business?' A lower multiple suggests relative cheapness; a higher multiple reflects the market's confidence in growth, moat, or stability.
computation: 1. Calculate or obtain Enterprise Value (sum of market cap, debt, preferred equity, minority interest, minus cash)
2. Extract trailing twelve-month (TTM) or forward EBITDA from financial statements or consensus estimates
3. Divide EV by EBITDA: multiple = EV / EBITDA in times

worked_example.problem: Compare valuations of two Indian industrial companies—one a premium consumer brand, one a cyclical commodity producer—using EV/EBITDA to isolate operating quality.
steps: Asian Paints FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,90,000 Cr, EBITDA ≈ ₹6,800 Cr → EV/EBITDA = 42.6x

Interpret Asian Paints: Extraordinarily rich valuation. Justified by 30%+ ROCE, durable structural growth in Indian paints demand, powerful brand moat, and 15+ years of compounding. Market is paying 42.6 years of current EBITDA, implying strong belief in multi-year growth.
Tata Steel FY23: EV ≈ ₹2,50,000 Cr, EBITDA ≈ ₹28,000 Cr → EV/EBITDA = 8.9x

Interpret Tata Steel: Cyclical commodity valuation. Market refuses to pay a premium multiple because steel EBITDA is hostage to global commodity cycles and Chinese supply. Same rupee amount of EBITDA as Asian Paints generates 4.8x less value.
worked_example.result: Asian Paints 42.6x vs. Tata Steel 8.9x — a 4.8x differential despite similar absolute EBITDA in rupee terms, purely because of business quality and cyclicality.
worked_example.insight: Benchmark rule of thumb for Indian markets: cyclical commodity businesses 5–10x, stable manufacturing 10–14x, consumer staples with moat 25–45x, luxury consumer and premium brands 40–60x, software/tech 25–50x depending on growth. Asian Paints at 42.6x is at the top end of consumer staples—expensive but justified by its track record. Always pair EV/EBITDA with growth expectations and ROCE to determine if a multiple is fair.

formulas.sensitivity_note: EV/EBITDA is the professional's default because it is capital-structure neutral and ignores non-cash depreciation. It works well for cross-company comparison. However, it understates the true cost of capex-heavy businesses (where depreciation is real economic cost). For capex-heavy industries, also look at EV/EBIT.

formulas.name: PEG Ratio
formulas.formula: PEG = P/E Ratio / Expected Earnings Growth Rate (%)

variables.meaning: Current or forward P/E ratio of the company
Expected annual EPS growth rate, typically a 2–3 year CAGR forward estimate as a percentage

formulas.plain_english: The PEG ratio adjusts the P/E multiple for expected earnings growth, recognising that a high P/E is justified if earnings are growing rapidly. It answers: 'Is this company's P/E premium proportional to its growth?'  Peter Lynch's rule of thumb: PEG below 1.0 suggests undervaluation, PEG 1.0–2.0 is fair, above 2.0 is expensive. However, PEG is only reliable for businesses with predictable, sustainable growth; cyclicals and turnarounds can be dangerous traps.
computation: 1. Obtain the current or forward P/E ratio
2. Obtain consensus or management guidance for 2–3 year EPS growth rate (as a percentage)
3. Divide P/E by growth rate: PEG = P/E / Growth Rate (%)

worked_example.problem: Compare two companies with different P/E multiples and growth rates to determine relative valuation using PEG.
steps: High-growth company (e.g., fintech unicorn): Forward P/E = 30x, expected EPS growth = 25% annually → PEG = 30 / 25 = 1.2
Cyclical company (e.g., Coal India): P/E = 6x, expected growth = 5% annually → PEG = 6 / 5 = 1.2
Superficial observation: Both have PEG = 1.2, so both appear equally valued.

Correct interpretation: The fintech at PEG 1.2 is attractive (paying for growth), but Coal India at PEG 1.2 is not (5% growth is cyclical, unreliable, and could reverse). PEG must always be paired with business quality and earnings visibility.
worked_example.result: PEG ratios are identical (1.2) but investment conclusions differ because one reflects sustainable growth, the other cyclical expansion.
worked_example.insight: PEG is powerful for identifying undervalued growth companies but treacherous for cyclicals. Always use multi-year (3+ year) forward growth estimates rather than single-year numbers to avoid being fooled by temporary earnings spikes. A coal or steel company showing strong near-term growth due to commodity price recovery will tempt value investors via low PEG—avoid this trap by stress-testing growth assumptions across a commodity cycle.

formulas.sensitivity_note: PEG works beautifully for growth stocks with predictable earnings trajectories but breaks down for cyclicals, turnarounds, or businesses with unreliable forward estimates. Always use multi-year (3-year+) growth estimates rather than single-year growth to avoid being fooled by one-off spikes.

formulas.name: P/S Ratio (Price-to-Sales)

variables.meaning: Current total equity market value
Trailing twelve-month (TTM) or forward annual revenue, also called Net Sales

formulas.plain_english: The P/S ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay for every rupee of revenue. It is the go-to metric for loss-making companies where P/E and PEG are meaningless. P/S is stable (harder to manipulate than earnings through accounting) but ignores profitability entirely—two companies with identical revenue but vastly different margins can trade at similar P/S but represent wildly different values. Always pair P/S with margin expectations.
computation: 1. Identify the company's current market cap
2. Obtain trailing twelve-month (TTM) or forward annual revenue from financial statements or consensus
3. Divide market cap by revenue: P/S = Market Cap / Revenue

worked_example.problem: Evaluate the valuation of a high-growth loss-making e-commerce/platform company using P/S where P/E is not applicable.
steps: Zomato FY23 (post-IPO): Market Cap at IPO ≈ ₹64,000 Cr, Revenue ≈ ₹4,200 Cr → P/S = 64,000 / 4,200 = 15.2x

Benchmark context: Amazon's early growth years (2005–2010) traded at 4–6x P/S. Zomato at 15x P/S represents the market pricing in: (a) rapid revenue growth in food delivery and adjacent services, (b) expectation of margin improvement over time, (c) optionality in advertising and fintech adjacencies.
Reality check: Zomato's net margin was negative at IPO (~-40%). At 15x P/S, the market was implicitly betting on reaching 3–5% net margins within 3–5 years, which would justify the valuation.
worked_example.result: Zomato at 15x P/S is expensive on an absolute basis but defensible for a high-growth platform if margin expansion materialises.
worked_example.insight: For loss-making growth companies, P/S is the entry point, but always overlay a margin bridge: 'What operating margin must this company achieve for the valuation to be fair?' If Zomato needs 10%+ net margins to justify 15x P/S but competitors in the space never exceed 3%, the valuation is a bet on disruption or monopoly pricing—a risky, concentrated call.

formulas.sensitivity_note: P/S ignores margin differences — a company with 30% operating margin and one with 5% margin can trade at similar P/S but have vastly different intrinsic values. Use P/S only as a starting point for loss-making companies; always overlay margin expectations before concluding.
